tasks.title: Beyond Teentaal
content: Teentaal, with its 16 beats in four equal groups, is the most common taal in Hindustani classical music. But it is only one of many rhythmic frameworks. Each taal creates a completely different rhythmic landscape, and learning several of them opens up a world of compositions, moods, and grooves that Teentaal alone cannot reach.

The taals every serious student should know are Jhaptaal (10 beats), Rupak (7 beats), Ektaal (12 beats), Dadra (6 beats), and Keherwa (8 beats). Each one has a unique internal structure - the way its beats are grouped into vibhags - and that grouping is what gives each taal its personality. Teentaal's even 4+4+4+4 feels square and stable. Jhaptaal's 2+3+2+3 swings. Rupak's 3+2+2 floats.
By the end of this room you will be able to recognise, count, and clap along with all of these taals - and understand why a composer would choose one over another.

tasks.title: Jhaptaal - 10 Beats
content: Jhaptaal has 10 matras divided into four vibhags with an asymmetric grouping: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3. This unevenness gives Jhaptaal a swinging, lilting quality that is very different from Teentaal's square four-by-four.
The clapping pattern is: tali (clap) on beats 1 and 3, khali (wave) on beat 6, and tali again on beat 8. Count it as: 1-2 (clap), 3-4-5 (clap), 6-7 (wave), 8-9-10 (clap).
The theka (basic drum pattern) is:
Dhi Na | Dhi Dhi Na | Ti Na | Dhi Dhi Na

Notice how the alternating groups of 2 and 3 create a push-and-pull feeling. The shorter 2-beat groups create urgency, while the 3-beat groups give space. This interplay is what makes Jhaptaal so musical.
Jhaptaal is widely used in classical vocal and instrumental compositions, especially in the madhya laya (medium tempo) range. Many famous bandishes are set in Jhaptaal.

tasks.title: Rupak - 7 Beats, Starting on Khali
content: Rupak has 7 matras in three vibhags grouped as 3 + 2 + 2. But its most striking feature is not the beat count - it is that sam (beat 1) falls on khali, the wave.

In every other common taal, sam is the strongest beat - the moment of emphasis, the landing point. In Rupak, sam is the lightest moment. Beat 1 is a wave, not a clap. The first tali (clap) does not arrive until beat 4.
This creates a unique feeling of suspension and delicacy. Where Teentaal's sam lands with authority, Rupak's sam floats. It is as if the music begins in mid-air.
The theka is:
Tin Tin Na | Dhi Na | Dhi Na
Notice the opening: Tin Tin Na - all light, treble strokes. The heavier Dhi strokes only appear in the second and third vibhags. The whole structure tilts away from weight on beat 1.

Rupak is used in many classical compositions and is especially suited to ragas with a gentle, introspective character. Its 7-beat cycle also creates interesting mathematical challenges for tihai calculations.

tasks.title: Ektaal - 12 Beats for Slow Compositions
content: Ektaal has 12 matras divided into six groups of 2. With four tali (clap) positions on beats 1, 5, 9, and 11, and two khali (wave) positions on beats 3 and 7, it has the most complex clapping pattern of the common taals.
The theka is:
Dhin Dhin | DhaGe TiRaKiTa | Tu Na | Ka Ta | DhaGe TiRaKiTa | Dhi Na

Ektaal is the taal of choice for vilambit (slow tempo) compositions in classical music. At a slow tempo, each of the 12 beats can last 2 to 5 seconds, stretching one full cycle to 30 seconds or even a minute. This enormous space between sam points gives the soloist room for extended improvisation.
The name 'Ektaal' means 'one taal' - reflecting its importance as a foundational rhythmic framework. Many of the greatest classical compositions are set in vilambit Ektaal.

At the vilambit tempo, counting Ektaal requires deep concentration. The tabla player's theka becomes a slow, meditative pattern that the soloist navigates like a river - knowing exactly where sam lies even when it feels very far away.

tasks.title: Dadra - The Simple Six
content: Dadra is the simplest of the common taals: 6 matras in two groups of 3. Tali on beat 1, khali on beat 4.
The theka is:
Dha Dhi Na | Dha Tin Na

Its 3+3 grouping creates a gentle, rocking motion - similar to a waltz in Western music. This natural, flowing feel makes Dadra the taal of choice for light classical genres like thumri and dadra (the genre shares the taal's name), as well as bhajans, folk songs, and many Bollywood compositions.

Despite its simplicity, Dadra is musically rich. The contrast between the first group (Dha Dhi Na - full, resonant strokes) and the second group (Dha Tin Na - the lighter Tin replacing Dhi) creates a satisfying breathing pattern within each cycle.
Because the cycle is so short (just 6 beats), sam arrives frequently. This makes Dadra feel grounded and accessible - you are never far from home.

tasks.title: Keherwa - 8 Beats for Light Music
content: Keherwa has 8 matras in two groups of 4. Tali on beat 1, khali on beat 5. Its structure is the simplest even-beat taal after Dadra.
The theka is:
Dha Ge Na Ti | Na Ka Dhi Na

Keherwa is everywhere in Indian music. It is the default rhythm for bhajans (devotional songs), ghazals (Urdu poetry set to music), qawwali, and a huge number of film songs. If you have ever clapped along to a Bollywood song, chances are you were clapping in Keherwa.

Its 4+4 structure shares the same even feel as Teentaal's vibhags, but with only 8 beats the cycle is half as long. This makes it feel more direct and propulsive - less room for complex rhythmic development, but more energy and forward motion.

Keherwa is also the taal that many students encounter first when learning to play along with recorded music, because its cycle is short enough to track easily and it appears in so many familiar songs.

tasks.title: Understanding Bols
content: Every taal's theka is written in bols - syllables that represent specific strokes on the tabla. The tabla has two drums: the smaller dayan (treble, right hand) and the larger bayan (bass, left hand). Each bol tells the tabla player exactly which drum to strike and how.
The main bols you will encounter:
**Dha** - both drums struck together, open sound. The fullest, most resonant stroke. It anchors sam in most taals.
**Dhin** - both drums together with a ringing, sustained quality. Created by pressing the ring finger on the dayan while striking.
**Na** (or **Ta**) - dayan (treble) alone, open. A clean, bright stroke without bass.
**Tin** (or **Ti**) - dayan alone, lighter and thinner than Na. Used in khali sections to create contrast.
**Ge** (or **Ke**) - bayan (bass) alone. A deep, low sound.

These bols are onomatopoeia - they sound like the strokes they describe. When you say 'Dha' aloud, the combination of the D and the aspirated 'ha' mimics the sound of both drums struck together. When you say 'Tin', the thin, high 'i' sound mirrors the light treble stroke. This is why tabla students learn by reciting bols before ever touching the drums.

options.why: Bayan alone is Ge or Ke. Dha uses both drums.

options.why: A light treble stroke would be Tin or Ti. Dha involves both drums.

options.text: Because the syllables sound like the drum strokes they describe

options.text: Because they are always sung at the same pitch
options.why: Bols can be recited at any pitch. They are onomatopoeia because they imitate the drum sounds.

tasks.title: The Feel of Each Taal
content: Each taal has a distinct personality that comes from its vibhag grouping - the way its beats are divided into sections. This is not an abstract idea; you can feel it in your body when you clap along.
**Teentaal** (16 beats, 4+4+4+4): Square, stable, majestic. The even grouping creates a sense of order and balance. It suits everything from meditative alap to virtuosic drut compositions.
**Jhaptaal** (10 beats, 2+3+2+3): Swinging and lively. The alternating short and long groups create a sense of momentum and surprise. It suits compositions with energy and playfulness.

**Rupak** (7 beats, 3+2+2): Light, delicate, floating. The khali on sam removes the heaviness from beat 1, and the odd number of beats (7) prevents the cycle from feeling predictable. It suits ragas with an introspective character.
**Ektaal** (12 beats, 6 x 2): Expansive and meditative at slow tempo. The steady march of 2-beat groups creates a hypnotic pulse. At vilambit laya, it feels like a vast, slow ocean.
**Dadra** (6 beats, 3+3): Gentle and rocking, like a lullaby or a waltz. Its short cycle and simple structure make it accessible and warm. It suits light classical and devotional music.
**Keherwa** (8 beats, 4+4): Direct and propulsive. Similar to Teentaal's feel but more compact. It drives forward without the grandeur of 16 beats.

tasks.title: Clapping Challenge
content: The best way to internalise a taal is to clap it. The physical motion of clapping and waving connects your body to the rhythm in a way that counting alone cannot.
Practice these clapping patterns:
**Jhaptaal (10 beats):** Clap on 1, clap on 3, wave on 6, clap on 8. Count: 1-2 (clap), 3-4-5 (clap), 6-7 (wave), 8-9-10 (clap). Then repeat from 1.

**Rupak (7 beats):** Wave on 1, clap on 4, clap on 6. Count: 1-2-3 (wave), 4-5 (clap), 6-7 (clap). Then repeat from 1. The wave on beat 1 will feel strange at first - your instinct is to clap on the downbeat.
**Dadra (6 beats):** Clap on 1, wave on 4. Count: 1-2-3 (clap), 4-5-6 (wave). Then repeat.
Start slowly. Say the beat numbers aloud while clapping. Once the pattern is automatic, try speaking the theka bols while clapping - this is how Indian music students train.
